A chat with Dino Magistrati, founder of the Museo Etnografico della Val Trebbia at Callegari (Bobbio), president of the Fondazione Fabrizio Bertuzzi e Mina Losi and former president of the Comunità Montana Appennino Piacentino, painter and contemporary artist; but, above all, a devotee of the memory of rural civilisation and of a world that is disappearing

Dear Dino, first of all I would ask you to explain to us what drives the existence of your peasant Museum…

Sheer madness.

What do you mean?

It’s true. In my family’s old farmhouses there was not only a heritage of rural archaeology, but also a formidable inventory of farm tools. The idea of the Museum came to me in a flash. Since 2000 it has been a temple of peasant material culture, which has always been ill-treated because it was considered “second-rate” culture, or even “non-culture”.

Anyone who knocks about Emilia can hardly fail to think of the Museo Guatelli at Ozzano Taro…

A wonderful place and a fantastic project. But there is a big difference: I only put on display what bears witness to what life was like in the days of the peasant world: work, cooking, know-how, the passing of the day and of time. Ettore Guatelli was a giant, who based his thinking on deep reflections linked to the pleasure of accumulating objects and to the infinite potential of their reuse. However, this approach has also led to some excesses: the prostitution of historical memory at flea markets, the “consumption” of memories reduced to gadgets and the loss of the bond between the object and its context. In short, the disappearance of the soul. It is the antechamber of the rubbish dump.

But I’m sure there are also several things you have in common.

Yes, at least one: the urgency of saving objects, things, memories. They look at us and ask us to save them: in the whole world, there are at least two of us, Ettore Guatelli and I, who have answered this call.

All right, but what if you had to explain to a five-year-old why these things deserve to be saved?

I would tell him that agriculture was the first step of our civilisation: everything that belongs to it must be safeguarded and studied; it is the foundation of our civilisation and of all the connections that humanity has built on top of it.

So it isn’t nostalgia?

No. The spaces, the tools, the household objects were the fruit of labour, ingenuity and creativity. These are values in themselves, in every age, forever. The stones of our houses here at Callegari, carried along winding mule tracks, tell us a story of toil. The use of many tools goes back to the dawn of time, or nearly: the plough, the billhook, the manarese…

Every year, on the second Sunday of June, you bring back to life the Cantando in Corte festival, a celebration of your Museum and of the activities connected with it.

It’s a way of keeping attention alive… in a setting that has grown poorer. The average age in our area is over 60, agriculture is on its knees, there is no tourism and perhaps that’s just as well, given the effect it has elsewhere. My family and I try to nurture a memory of the places where people lived, without distorting them.

How would you rate the public’s response to the festival?

Over time, it has improved. Let me give you an example: when you came last year to talk about your book, about the decline of the rural landscape and the annihilation of our roots, the audience was extremely receptive. But you seem to be the only one of your age who keeps going! Then again, the project to rediscover the Antica Via del Cifalco proves it. Beautiful, important. Honestly, when you first told me about it, I didn’t think you would pull it off. You have been more than stubborn.

Thank you, Dino. But now please, go on.

Visitors are more and more aware, but there are fewer and fewer of them… because many have ended up in the cemetery! There is no generational turnover: just as young people desert the mountains, it is only natural that they lose interest in their material culture. Typically, around the Museum, which by the way doesn’t get a scrap of help or funding from anyone, I have always tried to build up a group of volunteers. But I have never managed it, because… there aren’t any.

The abandonment of our mountains is well known and goes back a long way. But why are these places, which seem so poetic to us, so unattractive?

The neglect is general and at every level. In our communities, there is a lack of facilities and of work. Here at Callegari we don’t even have fibre optic broadband. And yet we’re hardly in the Himalayas. Without this kind of basic service, people leave. The roots that were ours are no longer those of today’s young people, because they no longer recognise them as such. These places are no longer theirs, and the cult of memory – even as such – has been lost.

You have long experience in municipal and provincial administration, as well as in the Comunità Montana. What can/should public institutions do?

They can certainly do a great deal more, even with the resources – meagre, to tell the truth – that they already have. But the point is to do better rather than to do more. If you cannot act sensibly, you are better off staying still, because every year precious resources are thrown to the wind on nonsense.

Let me guess: you’re thinking of the so-called “modernisation” of the Statale 45 road.

You read my mind.

So, what do we say to those who tell us that, to solve the problem of mountain depopulation, we need to build expressways through the gentle Emilian hills, devastating valleys of priceless environmental and landscape value such as Val Trebbia?

This project is one of the faces of evil. I’ll add nothing more, except that in the 1900s they had thought of building a railway. If this is the result today, perhaps the idea of 100 years ago was better.

An example, instead, of how public institutions could help more concretely to support the memory of places?

I’ll give you one right away: I had to ask for my Museum to be included on the official website of the Comune di Bobbio, and do you know what? It took me 25 years to get it and, even now, you need a computer engineer to find the dedicated page on the site! Sometimes it would take so little…

But then again, Bobbio has the cinema now…

Exactly, that’s my point. But all that glitters is not gold. In fact, real gold often doesn’t glitter at all.
